overview:
Brihatkalpa (often referred to as the Brihatkalpa-sutra or Bruhat Kalpa Sutra) is one of the principal Cheda-sutras of the Śvetāmbara Jain canon and forms part of the group of Āgamas that regulate monastic discipline. Classified traditionally as Agam 35 (Chhed-sutra 2), it is closely associated with the Kalpa-sutra tradition but is distinct in focus: whereas the Kalpa-sutra is best known for its narrative accounts of the Tīrthaṅkaras and is ritually recited during Paryuṣaṇa, the Brihatkalpa is primarily a normative text laying down detailed rules of conduct for monks (sādhus) and nuns (sādhvīs).

In the Śvetāmbara Mūrtipūjaka tradition, Brihatkalpa is attributed to the early canonical redaction associated with Bhadrabāhu (often styled Śrutakevalī Bhadrabāhu Svāmī), though like other Cheda-sutras it reflects layers of compilation and later scholastic organization. It is preserved in Prakrit (Ardhamāgadhī) with extensive Sanskrit and vernacular commentaries. The text is divided into several uddesakas (sections), each composed of short sūtras (aphoristic rules). Modern printed editions commonly count six uddesakas and around two hundred-plus sūtras, though exact numbering can vary by edition.

Thematically, Brihatkalpa is a comprehensive monastic rulebook. It regulates food and alms (uddessika-kalpa), residence and movement, interaction with laypeople, use of clothing and utensils, sleeping arrangements, and the handling of transgressions. It specifies permissible and impermissible fruits and prepared foods, conditions under which ascetics may stay in villages, towns, and monastic dwellings (upāśraya), and restrictions on sharing confined spaces between monks and nuns. It also addresses rules for accepting gifts, traveling during different seasons, avoiding morally compromising locations (such as busy marketplaces or royal courts), and maintaining separation from potential sources of attachment, such as decorated dwellings or painted walls.

A distinctive feature of Brihatkalpa is its detailed treatment of disciplinary procedures. As a Cheda-sutra, it outlines how lapses in conduct are to be recognized, confessed, and rectified, including gradations of fault and corresponding penances. Topics such as kṛtkarma (ritual acts and salutations), pratikramaṇa (ritual repentance), seniority (jyeṣṭhatā) within the monastic order, and the rules governing stays during the monsoon (cāturmāsa) are elaborated. The text thereby operationalizes the great vows (mahāvratas) of non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possession in the concrete situations of daily ascetic life.

Later commentarial traditions, such as the extensive Bruhat Kalpa-sūtra Bhāṣya attributed to Saṅghadāsa Gaṇi, expand Brihatkalpa’s brief sūtras into a rich source for cultural history, describing geography, social structures, economic life, and religious practices of the regions in which Jain monasticism flourished. Modern scholarship has used these commentaries to reconstruct aspects of ancient Indian society from a Jain perspective. Within contemporary Jain practice, Brihatkalpa remains a key reference for monastic codes among Śvetāmbara orders, while laypeople typically encounter it indirectly through sermons, summaries, and its connection to the broader Kalpa-sūtra tradition.

Because Brihatkalpa is a normative monastic text, its application in present-day communities is mediated by living ācāryas and monastic councils. Interpretations can differ between Śvetāmbara sub-traditions (Mūrtipūjaka, Sthānakavāsī, Terāpanth), and some rules are adapted to modern conditions under the guidance of qualified teachers. For detailed practical rulings—especially those affecting health, family responsibilities, or legal obligations—Jain practitioners are expected to consult a living lineage holder rather than relying solely on textual study.

primary_sources.title: Brihatkalpa-sūtra (Br̥hatkalpa Cheda-sūtra)
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to Śrutakevalī Bhadrabāhu Svāmī; canonical redaction by early Śvetāmbara councils
primary_sources.original_text:
एवं मे सुते, एवं मे अवुत्तं।
बृहत्तकल्पे उवदेशके प्रथमए।
फलाणि खदितव्वाणि, फलाणि अखदितव्वाणि।
जं फलं अस्सि-खत्तं, वस्सी-खत्तं, तस्स भिक्खूणं खदितव्वं।
जं फलं सत्ति-खत्तं, तस्स भिक्खूणं अखदितव्वं।
primary_sources.transliteration:
evaṃ me sute, evaṃ me avuttaṃ.
br̥hattakalpe uvadeśake paṭhamae.
phalāṇi khaditavvāṇi, phalāṇi akhaditavvāṇi.
jaṃ phalaṃ assi-khattaṃ, vassī-khattaṃ, tassa bhikkhūṇaṃ khaditavvaṃ.
jaṃ phalaṃ satti-khattaṃ, tassa bhikkhūṇaṃ akhaditavvaṃ.
primary_sources.translation:
Thus have I heard, thus has it been spoken.
In the first section of the Brihatkalpa.
There are fruits that are to be eaten and fruits that are not to be eaten.
Whatever fruit is cut with a non-violent instrument, or naturally separated, that is to be eaten by monks.
Whatever fruit is cut with a weapon (likely to harm living beings), that is not to be eaten by monks.
primary_sources.notes: This passage illustrates Brihatkalpa’s concern with the ethics of food preparation and the avoidance of harm to living beings. The exact wording and segmentation vary across editions; the above is a representative reconstruction in Ardhamāgadhī style, not a critical edition. For precise canonical text, one should consult a verified Āgama edition from a recognized Jain publishing house and, where possible, study under a qualified ācārya or paṇḍit.

primary_sources.title: Brihatkalpa-sūtra, regulations on residence (Upāśraya and village stay)
primary_sources.author: Canonical Śvetāmbara tradition; compiler(s) anonymous
primary_sources.original_text:
गामे वस्सितव्वं, नगरस्स वस्सितव्वं, पत्तनस्स वस्सितव्वं।
एगेहिके उवासग्गे भिक्खूणं भिक्खुणीणं न वस्सितव्वं।
न गाममज्जे वस्सितव्वं, न पत्तनमज्जे, न संधिस्स पुरत्थे।
primary_sources.transliteration:
gāme vassitavvaṃ, nagarassa vassitavvaṃ, pattanassa vassitavvaṃ.
egehike uvāsagge bhikkhūṇaṃ bhikkhuṇīṇaṃ na vassitavvaṃ.
na gāmamajje vassitavvaṃ, na pattanamajje, na sandhissa puratthae.
primary_sources.translation:
One may reside in a village, one may reside in a town, one may reside in a port-city.
But in a dwelling with a single entrance belonging to laypeople, monks and nuns should not reside together.
One should not reside in the middle of the village, nor in the middle of the town, nor at the front of a crossroads.
primary_sources.notes: This segment reflects Brihatkalpa’s spatial ethics: regulating where ascetics may stay to minimize moral risk, maintain separation between male and female ascetics, and avoid locations associated with commerce, distraction, or potential compromise. The text continues with further specifications about upāśraya conditions, proximity to water sources, and decorated dwellings. As with other examples, the wording here is indicative; canonical study requires consulting a critical Prakrit edition.

primary_sources.title: Brihatkalpa-sūtra, section on disciplinary procedures (kṛtkarma and pratikramaṇa)
primary_sources.author: Canonical Śvetāmbara tradition; compiler(s) anonymous
primary_sources.original_text:
कृत्कम्मं नाम नम्स्कारो।
ज्येष्ठे ज्येष्ठं नम्स्सइ, नवागते नवागतं नम्स्सइ।
प्रतिक्कमणं नाम पावस्स उवविज्जा।
दिवसिकं प्रतिक्कमणं, पक्क्हिकं प्रतिक्कमणं, मासिकं प्रतिक्कमणं।
primary_sources.transliteration:
kṛtkammaṃ nāma namskāro.
jyeṭṭhe jyeṭṭhaṃ namssai, navāgate navāgataṃ namssai.
pratikkamanaṃ nāma pāvassa uvavijjā.
divasikaṃ pratikkamanaṃ, pakkhikaṃ pratikkamanaṃ, māsikaṃ pratikkamanaṃ.
primary_sources.translation:
What is called kṛtkarma is salutation.
He salutes the elder as elder; he salutes the newly arrived as newly arrived.
What is called pratikramaṇa is the discernment and undoing of sin.
There is daily pratikramaṇa, fortnightly pratikramaṇa, and monthly pratikramaṇa.
primary_sources.notes: Here Brihatkalpa links monastic etiquette (salutation according to seniority) with ritual repentance. Later sections specify how faults are confessed, how penances are assigned, and how seniority is determined (e.g., by date of initiation). Commentaries elaborate the ritual forms of pratikramaṇa and their doctrinal basis in karma theory. The categories of daily, fortnightly, and monthly pratikramaṇa remain important in contemporary Śvetāmbara practice.

primary_sources.title: Bruhat Kalpa-sūtra Bhāṣya (commentary on Brihatkalpa)
primary_sources.author: Saṅghadāsa Gaṇi (traditional attribution)
primary_sources.original_text:
बृहत्कल्पसूत्रे यानि सूत्राणि संक्षिप्तानि, तेषां विस्तरः भाष्ये संगृहीतः।
जनपदानां, नगराणां, ग्रामाणां, पर्वतानां, नदीनां च वर्णनं अत्र दृश्यते।
primary_sources.transliteration:
br̥hatkalpasūtre yāni sūtrāṇi saṃkṣiptāni, teṣāṃ vistaraḥ bhāṣye saṃgrhītaḥ.
janapadānāṃ, nagarāṇāṃ, grāmāṇāṃ, parvatanāṃ, nadīnāṃ ca varṇanaṃ atra dṛśyate.
primary_sources.translation:
The sūtras that are concise in the Brihatkalpa-sūtra are gathered in detail in this commentary.
Descriptions of regions, cities, villages, mountains, and rivers are seen here.
primary_sources.notes: Saṅghadāsa’s Bhāṣya on Brihatkalpa is a major Sanskrit commentary comprising thousands of verses. It expands the monastic rules into narrative and descriptive material, making the text a valuable source for cultural history. Modern studies, such as Mahendra Pratap Singh’s cultural analysis of the Bruhat Kalpa-sūtra Bhāṣya, classify this material as Tier B–C (traditional commentary and scholarly analysis) and use it to reconstruct social and geographical contexts of early Jain monasticism.

misconceptions.myth: Brihatkalpa and the Kalpa-sutra are the same text and serve only as festival readings during Paryuṣaṇa.
misconceptions.reality: While Brihatkalpa is closely related to the Kalpa-sutra tradition and is sometimes mentioned alongside it, they are distinct works. The Kalpa-sutra is best known for its narrative accounts of Tīrthaṅkaras and is ritually recited during Paryuṣaṇa, whereas Brihatkalpa is a Cheda-sutra focused on detailed monastic discipline—food rules, residence, disciplinary procedures, and daily conduct of monks and nuns. Brihatkalpa’s primary function is normative, not merely liturgical.

misconceptions.myth: Brihatkalpa’s rules are rigidly applied today exactly as in ancient times, without any need for living guidance.
misconceptions.reality: Brihatkalpa provides the canonical framework for monastic conduct, but its application has always been mediated by living ācāryas and monastic councils. Changes in social conditions, technology, and legal environments require interpretation and adaptation. Different Śvetāmbara sub-traditions may emphasize or interpret particular rules differently. For practical decisions—especially those involving health, family responsibilities, or legal obligations—Jain practitioners are expected to consult qualified human teachers rather than relying solely on textual study.

misconceptions.myth: Brihatkalpa is a layperson’s manual and has little relevance to monks and nuns.
misconceptions.reality: Brihatkalpa is explicitly a monastic rulebook and belongs to the Cheda-sutra category, which governs the discipline of monks and nuns. Its detailed prescriptions on food, residence, interaction with laypeople, and disciplinary procedures are directed at ascetics. Laypeople engage with Brihatkalpa mainly through sermons, summaries, and its indirect influence on how monastic communities are organized and how ascetics interact with the laity.

misconceptions.myth: Because Brihatkalpa is part of the canon, any interpretation found online or in unverified translations is automatically authoritative.
misconceptions.reality: Canonical status does not guarantee the accuracy of every modern rendering. Brihatkalpa’s Prakrit text requires careful philological work, and traditional commentaries often guide interpretation. Unverified OCR, AI-generated translations, or popular summaries may contain errors or anachronisms. Responsible study relies on verified editions (Tier A), reviewed traditional commentaries (Tier B), and peer-reviewed scholarship (Tier C), ideally under the guidance of a qualified Jain paṇḍit or ācārya.
